chemicals.concentration_notes: Celastrus scandens is generally regarded as low toxicity; the specific toxin in cats is not well established (Pet Poison Helpline).
chemicals.description: ASPCA lists the toxic principles as cardenolides and alkaloids. Ingestion mainly irritates the gastrointestinal tract, producing vomiting and diarrhea; large ingestions may cause weakness and, rarely, seizures.
chemicals.name: Cardenolides and alkaloids

description: American Bittersweet (Celastrus scandens) is a vigorous woody vine native to North America, easily recognised by its orange-yellow berries that split open to reveal bright red seeds. All parts of the plant are toxic to cats, including the leaves, bark, roots, berries, and seeds. ASPCA lists the toxic principles as cardenolides and alkaloids; the plant mainly irritates the gastrointestinal tract. Toxicity is generally low, with mild self-limiting signs such as vomiting and diarrhea, and rarely weakness or seizures after large ingestions. The vivid berries are the most likely point of contact for cats, particularly when the vine is brought indoors as a decorative autumn cutting.
emergencyNote: Induction of Emesis (Vomiting) or Gastric Lavage
name: Bittersweet
safetyNotes: Symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain from GI irritation; larger exposures may cause lethargy, muscle weakness, and rarely seizures.
Berries are the primary hazard: Brightly coloured and accessible, the berries are appealing to curious cats — avoid using the plant as indoor decoration.
Action: Seek veterinary care if more than a small berry has been ingested, particularly if lethargy or weakness develops.

symptoms.name: Vomiting and Diarrhea
symptoms.notes: These are often the first signs of ingestion. The plant irritates the gastrointestinal tract (ASPCA: vomiting, diarrhea).

symptoms.name: Weakness and Lethargy
symptoms.notes: Larger ingestions may cause weakness and lethargy (ASPCA; Pet Poison Helpline).
symptoms.onset: 2–24 hours (typically follows or accompanies GI signs).

symptoms.name: Seizures (rare)
symptoms.notes: Seizures are reported only rarely and usually with large ingestions (ASPCA; Pet Poison Helpline).

treatments.description: If the ingestion was recent (typically within 1–2 hours) and the cat is not showing severe symptoms, the veterinarian may induce vomiting using medication (such as xylazine for cats) to remove the plant material from the stomach. Alternatively, gastric lavage (stomach pumping) may be performed under anesthesia to wash out the stomach contents.
treatments.name: Induction of Emesis (Vomiting) or Gastric Lavage
treatments.notes: This is the primary defense to prevent further toxin absorption. It is only performed if the ingestion is recent and the cat is neurologically stable. Self-medication or inducing vomiting at home is not recommended; immediate veterinary intervention is required.

treatments.description: The administration of medical-grade activated charcoal (1–4 g/kg body weight) into the digestive tract. This substance binds unabsorbed toxins in the gut, preventing them from entering the bloodstream.
treatments.name: Activated Charcoal Administration
treatments.notes: In significant ingestions, administration may be repeated at 4 to 6-hour intervals to limit ongoing toxin absorption.

treatments.description: The administration of crystalloid solutions directly into the vein to rehydrate the cat and maintain electrolyte balance.
treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluid Therapy
treatments.notes: This step helps in two ways: 1) To compensate for dehydration caused by vomiting and diarrhea. 2) To stimulate diuresis (urination), which promotes the excretion of toxins and supports the kidneys.

treatments.description: Using specific medications to manage symptoms as they arise. Benzodiazepines or barbiturates may be used to control seizures in the rare cases where they occur.
treatments.name: Drug Therapy (Anticonvulsants)
treatments.notes: There is no specific antidote. Treatment is supportive and focuses on controlling GI signs and, rarely, seizures.
